--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.small_world_sigma()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute the small-world coefficient sigma. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.small_world_sigma()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute the small-world coefficient sigma. title: >- [Graph.small_world_sigma()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Compute the small-world coefficient sigma. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the small-world coefficient sigma. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L37027-L37161){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.small_world_sigma( iterations=100, nrand=10, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Small-world coefficient sigma](../assets/graphs/small-world-sigma.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="An eight-node ring with four chords that close four triangles. Its transitivity C is 0.43, against 0.354 averaged over 10 degree-preserving random references, while its average path length L, 1.643, is close to the references' 1.707. The card divides the two ratios, (0.43 / 0.354) / (1.643 / 1.707), for sigma = 1.260: above 1, so the graph counts as small-world." width="100%"} A small-world network combines the high clustering of a lattice with the short paths of a random graph. Humphries and Gurney (2008) measure this as $$\sigma = \frac{C / C_r}{L / L_r},$$ where $C$ is the transitivity and $L$ the average shortest path length, and $C_r$, $L_r$ are their averages over `nrand` random reference graphs with the same degrees (see `random_reference()`). A network is commonly called small-world when $\sigma > 1$: clustered well beyond chance while keeping near-random path lengths. Typical uses are brain, social and infrastructure networks. The graph must be undirected and connected, and is treated as simple. The result is random; use `seed=` for reproducible values. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [iterations]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Rewiring rounds for each random reference (default 100, as in NetworkX). [nrand]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[10]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of random references to average (default 10). [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The coefficient sigma. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or disconnected, or has fewer than four nodes or two edges. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Follows NetworkX's `sigma`, with the rewiring and the metrics computed in Rust, which makes it practical on graphs of a few thousand nodes (each reference needs all-pairs breadth-first searches for $L_r$). Because the references are random, values from EdgeCase and NetworkX agree only up to sampling noise. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~small_world_omega`) : Place a graph between a lattice and a random graph. [](`~random_reference`) : The random graphs that sigma compares against. [](`~transitivity`) : The clustering that sigma uses. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A ring lattice with a few edges rewired keeps most of its clustering, while the shortcuts make its paths short: ::: {#fb20962b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=60, k=6, p=0.05, seed=1) round(graph.small_world_sigma(seed=1), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5.34 ``` ::: ::: ### From a lattice to a random graph Watts and Strogatz (1998) rewired a ring lattice a little at a time. Sigma peaks after a little rewiring, at 5.3, then falls toward 1 as the graph turns random. It rates the unrewired ring highly too, at 3.5: its clustering is far above chance, which outweighs paths more than twice as long. `small_world_omega()` tells those two apart: ::: {#8a60b1cf .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl rings = { p: ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=60, k=6, p=p, seed=1) for p in [0.0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0] } pl.DataFrame({ "p": list(rings), "clustering": [ g.average_clustering_coefficient() for g in rings.values() ], "sigma": [g.small_world_sigma(seed=1) for g in rings.values()], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ### Two real networks `celegans_neural()` is the network of a worm's neurons that Watts and Strogatz used. As an undirected graph, it is clearly small-world, at about 1.5. The karate club is only just above 1. Sigma takes `nrand` references, each rewired `iterations` times per edge, so on larger graphs it pays to lower them: ::: {#c3529194 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} worm = ec.celegans_neural().to_undirected() ( worm.small_world_sigma(iterations=10, nrand=5, seed=1), ec.karate_club().small_world_sigma(seed=1), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (1.526696835772174, 1.1234102684879885) ``` ::: :::
